anchor.title: U.S. Supreme Court Building, Washington, D.C. (c. 1939)
anchor.creator: Farm Security Administration / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: Farm Security Administration. "U.S. Supreme Court Building, Washington, D.C." 1939. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (LCCN 2017878871), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U.S._Supreme_Court_building,_Washington,_D.C._LCCN2017878871.jpg.
anchor.alt: Color photograph from around 1939 of the white marble United States Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C., with tall classical Corinthian columns and a paved walkway leading to the entrance.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows the United States Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C., around 1939, with its white marble columns and the words 'Equal Justice Under Law' carved above the entrance. The Supreme Court is the highest court in the country, and it is where the justices decide whether laws follow the Constitution. Inside this building in 1954, the Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that separating students by race in public schools was unconstitutional. That decision helped begin the modern Civil Rights Movement. The building reminds us that many civil rights battles were fought and won through the courts.

anchor.title: Martin Luther King Jr. at Press Conference Lectern (March 26, 1964)
anchor.creator: Marion S. Trikosko, U.S. News & World Report Magazine
anchor.citation: Trikosko, Marion S. "Martin Luther King Jr. at Press Conference Lectern." 26 Mar. 1964. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, U.S. News & World Report Magazine Collection (LC-DIG-ppmsc-01269), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Martin-Luther-King-1964-leaning-on-a-lectern.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white close-up photograph from March 1964 of the Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. leaning forward on a lectern at a press conference, his expression earnest and direct.
anchor.caption: This photograph from March 1964 shows the Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. speaking at a press conference, leaning forward on a lectern with a serious, focused expression. King was the best-known leader of the Civil Rights Movement, and he believed in nonviolent protest to change unjust laws. He led major campaigns such as the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the March on Washington, where he gave his famous 'I Have a Dream' speech. The photograph was taken in 1964, the same year he won the Nobel Peace Prize and the Civil Rights Act was passed. The close-up view helps us see King as a real person and leader, not just a name in a textbook.

anchor.title: Rosa Parks Seated at Front of Montgomery Bus After Boycott Victory (December 21, 1956)
anchor.creator: United Press International (UPI) wire photo
anchor.citation: United Press International. "Rosa Parks Seated at Front of Montgomery Bus After Boycott Victory." 21 Dec. 1956. Via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rosa_Parks_on_bus_on_December_21,_1956.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph from December 21, 1956, of Rosa Parks seated near the front of a Montgomery, Alabama, city bus, with a man seated behind her.
anchor.caption: This photograph from December 1956 shows Rosa Parks sitting near the front of a city bus in Montgomery, Alabama, on the day the bus boycott ended. A year earlier, Parks had been arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger. In response, Black residents of Montgomery refused to ride the buses for over a year, until the Supreme Court ruled that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott was led by the young Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and showed the power of peaceful, organized protest. Parks sitting at the front of the bus represents the victory the protest finally achieved.

anchor.title: President Johnson Signs the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (July 2, 1964)
anchor.creator: Cecil Stoughton, White House Press Office
anchor.citation: Stoughton, Cecil. "President Johnson Signs the Civil Rights Act of 1964." 2 July 1964. Executive Office of the President / White House, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lyndon_Johnson_signing_Civil_Rights_Act,_July_2,_1964.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph from July 2, 1964, of President Lyndon B. Johnson seated at a desk in the White House signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, surrounded by legislators and civil rights leaders including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in the background.
anchor.caption: This photograph from July 2, 1964, shows President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964 at the White House. Around him stand members of Congress and civil rights leaders, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The new law made it illegal to discriminate against people because of their race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in jobs and public places. It was the most important civil rights law since the end of slavery and Reconstruction. The photograph shows how years of protest finally led to a major change in the law.

anchor.title: César Chávez Interview Portrait (April 20, 1979)
anchor.creator: Marion S. Trikosko, U.S. News & World Report Magazine
anchor.citation: Trikosko, Marion S. "César Chávez Interview Portrait." 20 Apr. 1979. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, U.S. News & World Report Magazine Collection (LC-DIG-ppmsca-56576), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cesar_Chavez_40913a.tif.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph from April 20, 1979, of César Chávez, the United Farm Workers labor leader, seated at a table and looking down at a document during an interview.
anchor.caption: This photograph from 1979 shows César Chávez, a labor leader, seated at a table and reading a document during an interview. Chávez co-founded the United Farm Workers union and organized mostly Mexican American and Filipino American farm workers in California. He used nonviolent methods like strikes, marches, and boycotts to demand fair pay and better working conditions, most famously during the Delano grape strike that began in 1965. Working with organizers such as Dolores Huerta, he was a key leader of the Chicano Movement. His work shows that the fight for civil rights included Latino communities and workers, not only African Americans.
